title: Keys, key signatures, and the circle of fifths
description: Memorize sharp and flat orders, signature-reading shortcuts, and fifth shapes on string 6 to 5.

cards.front: What is a key? What is tonality?
cards.back: A key is a set of pitch classes organized around one tonic — the note that feels like home. Tonality is that organization: some notes and chords resolve toward others, and the tonic is where they resolve.

cards.front: What does a key signature tell you, and what does it not tell you by itself?
cards.back: It lists the sharps or flats every note of that name receives, so you know which seven-letter collection is in use. It does not, by itself, tell you the tonic: the same signature belongs to a major key and its relative minor.

cards.front: What does the circle of fifths arrange, and how do neighbours differ?
cards.back: The twelve keys, so that neighbours differ by exactly one accidental.

cards.front: Using tetrachords, why does moving from C major to G major add only F♯?
cards.back: The upper tetrachord of C major is G A B C, which is the lower tetrachord of G major. The new upper tetrachord starts on D: D E F♯ G. The only change is F becoming F♯.

cards.front: What accidental is added when you move up a perfect fifth? Down a perfect fifth?
cards.back: Up a fifth (C to G) adds one sharp, always on the new key’s degree 7. Down a fifth (C to F) adds one flat, always on the new key’s degree 4. The two collections share six of seven notes.

cards.front: What is the order of sharps?
cards.back: F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ E♯ B♯.

cards.front: What is the order of flats, and how does it relate to the sharps?
cards.back: B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭ C♭ F♭ — the sharps order reversed.

cards.front: List the major keys from 0 to 6 sharps and their accidentals.
cards.back: C none. G F♯. D F♯ C♯. A F♯ C♯ G♯. E F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯. B F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯. F♯ F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ E♯.

cards.front: List the major keys from 1 to 6 flats and their accidentals.
cards.back: F B♭. B♭ B♭ E♭. E♭ B♭ E♭ A♭. A♭ B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭. D♭ B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭. G♭ B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭ C♭.

cards.front: How are F♯ major and G♭ major related?
cards.back: They sound identical but are spelled differently. Both are real keys with different signatures (six sharps vs six flats).

cards.front: How do you read a sharp key from its signature?
cards.back: The last sharp in the order is degree 7. The tonic is a half step above it. Three sharps (last is G♯) means A.

cards.front: How do you read a flat key from its signature?
cards.back: The second-to-last flat is the tonic. Three flats (B♭ E♭ A♭): second-to-last is E♭. Exception: one flat is F, which you memorize.

cards.front: Why are circle neighbours closely related, and what are C major’s neighbours as chords?
cards.back: Only one note changes. C major’s neighbours G and F supply its most important chords: G is V (dominant) and F is IV (subdominant). Most songs modulate to a neighbour first.

cards.front: Why is the circle also a map of strong progressions?
cards.back: Descending-fifth motion (C → F, or A → D → G) is one of the most common root movements in tonal music.

cards.front: From a root on string 6 at fret r, where is a fifth up? A fifth down?
cards.back: Up a fifth: string 5, fret r+2. Down a fifth (same as up a fourth): string 5, fret r.

cards.front: From C at string 6 fret 8, where are G and F on string 5?
cards.back: G at string 5 fret 10 (fifth up). F at string 5 fret 8 (fifth down). Both are neighbours on the circle.

cards.front: On which string pairs is “up a fourth” the same fret, and where does that rule break?
cards.back: Same fret one string toward string 1 for 6–5, 5–4, and 4–3 (E→A→D→G). The 3–2 pair (G→B) is only a major third, so do not extend the rule across that pair.

cards.front: A song uses C, G, and D. Which is the likely tonic, and how do you confirm?
cards.back: They are three adjacent keys; the middle one, G, is the likely tonic, with C as IV and D as V. G, C, D, Em, and Am all use only G major (F♯). F or B♭ does not fit. Confirm by ear: the chord that settles is the tonic.

cards.front: Write the key signatures of A, E, B♭, and D♭ as lists of accidentals.
cards.back: F♯ C♯ G♯. F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯. B♭ E♭. B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭.

cards.front: Name the major key: 4 flats, 2 sharps, 5 sharps, 1 flat.
cards.back: A♭, D, B, F.

cards.front: Name the circle of fifths clockwise from C for all 12 keys.
cards.back: C G D A E B F♯ D♭ A♭ E♭ B♭ F. (F♯ and G♭ are the enharmonic pair at six accidentals.)

cards.front: Which two notes differ between D major and A major?
cards.back: Only G (in D) versus G♯ (in A). The new sharp is degree 7 of the new key.

cards.front: Root A on string 6 fret 5. Find E (fifth up) and D (fifth down) on string 5.
cards.back: String 5 fret 7 and string 5 fret 5.

cards.front: A song in D uses D G A Bm. Which chords are neighbours of D on the circle?
cards.back: G and A.
